g12-physics-up2-t1.overview: A thrown ball, a stone launched off a cliff, a basketball arcing toward the hoop — none of these move in a straight line, yet all obey two one-dimensional laws at once. This topic unpacks projectile motion: horizontal motion and vertical motion happen independently, stitched together only by time.
objectives: Resolve a launch velocity into horizontal and vertical components
Explain why horizontal and vertical motions are independent
Derive and use the trajectory equation y = x tanθ − gx²/(2v²cos²θ)
Calculate range and time of flight for a projectile
Show that range is maximum at 45° and equal for complementary angles
g12-physics-up2-t1.simple: Two motions, one ball. A projectile is anything thrown and then left to gravity alone. Horizontally it coasts at constant speed (no forces, so nothing to accelerate it); vertically it free-falls exactly like a dropped stone (vy = gt, y = ½gt²). The two know nothing about each other — they share only the clock. That single idea generates every formula in this topic, including why a 45° launch throws furthest.
g12-physics-up2-t1.detailed:
Independence of components. Galileo's insight: the horizontal motion of a projectile is unaffected by its vertical fall. A bullet fired horizontally and a bullet dropped from the same height hit the ground at the same instant (ignoring air and Earth curvature). We choose axes so ax = 0 and ay = g (downward), then treat the problem as two separate Unit-1 kinematics exercises running on the same stopwatch.

Component equations. Launch at speed v, angle θ: vx = v cosθ stays constant forever; vy = v sinθ − gt changes linearly; x = vt cosθ and y = vt sinθ − ½gt². At the top of the flight vy = 0 but vx is unchanged — the ball has not stopped, it has only finished rising. For a stone thrown horizontally, vy starts at 0 and grows as vy = gt while vx = v the whole way.

The trajectory. Eliminate t between x and y (t = x/(v cosθ)) and the path appears: y = x tanθ − gx²/(2v²cos²θ). Because the second term is proportional to x², the curve is a parabola — gravity writes the shape, the launch only picks the constants.

Range and time of flight. Set y = 0 to find where the projectile lands: time of flight T = 2v sinθ/g, and the horizontal distance covered is R = v²sin2θ/g. Since sin2θ peaks at 1 when θ = 45°, that is the maximum-range angle: R_max = v²/g. Because sin2θ = sin(180° − 2θ), a launch at 30° and one at 60° give identical range — the low flat shot and the high lofted shot land in the same spot, arriving at different times.

Basketball intuition. Why do players launch near 45–55° rather than 45°? The ball must enter the hoop from above at a steep-enough angle to open the target's effective area, and the release point sits above the rim's plane, so the textbook optimum shifts. Speed and angle trade off: shoot softer, arc higher; snap harder, flatten out. Physics explains the trade-off even when the exact optimum is sport-specific.

keyTerms.def: an object moving under the influence of gravity alone
vx = v cosθ, vy = v sinθ — the split of initial velocity
the parabolic path traced by a projectile
total air time, fixed by the vertical motion
θ and 90° − θ, which give equal range

formulas.when: every projectile, from the instant of release

formulas.name: Trajectory equation

workedExamples.problem: A stone is thrown horizontally at 20 m/s from the top of a 45 m cliff. When and where does it land? (g = 10 m/s²)
workedExamples.given: vy₀ = 0, x-direction speed vx = 20 m/s, drop height y = 45 m
workedExamples.calculation: Vertical: y = ½gt² → 45 = 5t² → t = 3 s. Horizontal: x = vx t = 20 × 3 = 60 m.
workedExamples.answer: It falls for 3 s and lands 60 m from the cliff base — the horizontal throw did not delay the fall at all.

workedExamples.problem: A ball is kicked at 20 m/s, 30° above horizontal (g = 10). Find time of flight, range and maximum height.
workedExamples.given: v₀ = 20 m/s, θ = 30°, so vy₀ = 10 m/s and vx₀ = 20cos30° ≈ 17.3 m/s
workedExamples.calculation: T = 2vy₀/g = 2 s. R = vx T = 17.3 × 2 ≈ 34.6 m. Peak height h = vy₀²/(2g) = 100/20 = 5 m.
workedExamples.answer: 2 s aloft, ≈ 34.6 m downrange, 5 m high at the top.

workedExamples.problem: Show that 30° and 60° launches at the same speed have equal range (R = v²sin2θ/g).
workedExamples.answer: Equal range, but the 60° shot stays in the air longer (T = 2v sinθ/g): 1.73 v/g vs 1.0 v/g.

workedExamples.problem: A gun fires horizontally at 100 m/s from a height of 1.25 m (g = 10). How far downrange does the bullet hit?
workedExamples.answer: 50 m. A bullet dropped from the same height would also take 0.5 s — independence in action.

commonMistakes: Assuming the projectile stops at the top of its arc — only vy is zero there; vx keeps going
Using time of flight T = 2v sinθ/g for launches off a cliff or from a height — that formula needs landing at launch level
Mixing g = 9.8 and g = 10 inside one calculation
Thinking a faster horizontal throw falls more slowly — vertical and horizontal motions are independent
Plugging θ into sin2θ as sin²θ or forgetting the factor of 2 in the range formula
applications: Sports: judging basketball arcs, football free-kicks and long-jump take-off angles
Ballistics and targeting: compensating drop over distance
Water jets and sprinkler design: arcs from angled nozzles
Road and avalanche barriers sized for the landing zone of rockfall treated as projectiles
g12-physics-up2-t1.summary: Split, solve, recombine: horizontal is constant velocity, vertical is free fall, and time is the only bridge. R = v²sin2θ/g peaks at 45°; complementary angles tie.

questions.q: Neglecting air resistance, the horizontal velocity of a projectile:
questions.explanation: No horizontal force acts, so vx never changes — even at the top of the arc.

questions.q: A ball rolls off a table at the same instant another ball is dropped from the table top. Which lands first (same height)?
questions.explanation: Both have vy₀ = 0 and fall the same height — vertical motion is independent of horizontal.

questions.q: The launch angle that gives maximum range on level ground is:
questions.explanation: R = v²sin2θ/g is largest when sin2θ = 1, i.e. θ = 45°.

questions.q: A projectile is launched at 20 m/s at 30° above level ground (g = 10). Its time of flight is:
Same launch (v = 20 m/s), angles 30° and 60°. Which statement is true? (g = 10)
questions.explanation: sin60° = sin120°, so ranges tie; but T ∝ sinθ, so the steeper shot hangs longer.

questions.q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 20 m/s from a 45 m cliff (g = 10). Where does it land?
For a projectile launched and landing at the same height, at the very top of its path:
options: velocity and acceleration are both zero
velocity is zero but acceleration is g
velocity is minimum but not zero, acceleration is g
questions.explanation: At the apex vy = 0 but vx survives, so speed is minimum, not zero; g acts throughout.

questions.q: A projectile has range equal to its maximum height on level ground. Its launch angle satisfies:
questions.explanation: R = H means v²sin2θ/g = v²sin²θ/(2g) → 2sinθcosθ = sin²θ/2 → tanθ = 4, so θ ≈ 76°.

g12-physics-up2-t2.overview: A grinding stone, a bicycle wheel, the Earth itself — spinning bodies trace circles, and every quantity of linear motion has an angular twin. This topic builds the language of rotation: radians, angular velocity and acceleration, and the kinematics equations that mirror Unit 1 almost line for line.
objectives: Define angular displacement in radians and convert between radians and degrees
Relate arc length and tangential speed to radius: s = rθ, v = rω
Compute average and instantaneous angular velocity and acceleration
Apply the rotational kinematics equations to constant-α problems
Explain the 'outward push' in a turning vehicle as inertia, not a real outward force
g12-physics-up2-t2.simple: Rotation is linear motion in disguise. Measure angles in radians, and every circular quantity is the straight-line one multiplied by the radius: distance becomes arc s = rθ, speed becomes v = rω. The constant-acceleration formulas return with Greek letters — ω = ω₀ + αt plays the role of v = v₀ + at. If you can do Unit 1 kinematics, you can already do this topic.
g12-physics-up2-t2.detailed:
The radian. One radian is the angle whose arc equals the radius. Since the full circumference is 2πr, a full turn is 2π rad = 360°, so 1 rad ≈ 57.3° and 1 rad = 180°/π. Radians are pure numbers (length ÷ length), which is why s = rθ works only when θ is in radians — degrees need a conversion factor and silently break formulas.

Angular velocity and acceleration. ω = Δθ/Δt (rad/s) says how fast the angle grows; every point on a rigid wheel shares the same ω. Linear speed, however, scales with radius: v = rω, so the outer edge of a grinding stone races while the hub barely moves. Changing spin rate gives α = Δω/Δt in rad/s². A record turntable at 33⅓ rpm has ω = 2π × 33.33/60 ≈ 3.5 rad/s.

Rotational kinematics (constant α). The dictionary is direct: θ↔x, ω↔v, α↔a. So ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ; θ = ½(ω₀ + ω)t. A wheel braking with α = −2 rad/s² from 20 rad/s stops in 10 s and turns through θ = ½ × 20 × 10 = 100 rad ≈ 15.9 revolutions on the way out.

Feeling 'thrown outward'. When a taxi takes a sharp turn in Addis, passengers feel pressed toward the outside door. In the ground (inertial) frame no outward force exists: your body simply keeps moving straight by inertia while the car turns beneath you, and the door is what finally pushes you inward. The outward 'centrifugal force' is a bookkeeping device used only in the rotating frame itself. The real, inward force needed to curve a path is centripetal: F = mv²/r.

Why the mirror works. A point on a spinning rim travels an arc s = rθ; multiplying that identity by ω and α converts it to v = rω and a_t = rα. Constant angular acceleration therefore inherits every linear derivation unchanged — memorise one set, own the other.

keyTerms.def: angle subtending an arc equal to the radius; 2π rad = 360°
rate of change of angle, Δθ/Δt in rad/s
rate of change of ω in rad/s²
linear speed of a point on the circle, v = rω
directed toward the centre; the net force that curves motion

formulas.name: Tangential speed

formulas.when: any point on a rigid rotating body

formulas.name: Radian conversion

formulas.name: Rotational kinematics (constant α)

workedExamples.problem: Convert 1 rev, 90° and 2.5 rad to the other angle units.
workedExamples.answer: Radian-first arithmetic: 1 rev = 2π rad exactly, and 1 rad ≈ 57.3°.

workedExamples.problem: A grinding stone of radius 0.25 m spins at 120 rpm. Find ω and the rim speed. (π ≈ 3.14)
workedExamples.answer: ω ≈ 12.6 rad/s; the rim (and a tool touching it) moves ≈ 3.1 m/s.

workedExamples.problem: A bicycle wheel spins down uniformly from 20 rad/s to rest in 10 s. Find α and the number of revolutions made while stopping.
workedExamples.answer: α = −2 rad/s²; about 16 revolutions before it stops.

workedExamples.problem: Two points sit at r = 0.1 m and r = 0.4 m on the same turntable spinning at ω = 5 rad/s. Compare their speeds and their angular velocities.
workedExamples.calculation: v₁ = 0.1 × 5 = 0.5 m/s; v₂ = 0.4 × 5 = 2 m/s — the outer point is 4× faster. Both share ω = 5 rad/s.
workedExamples.answer: Same ω everywhere on a rigid body; v grows in direct proportion to r.

commonMistakes: Plugging degrees into s = rθ or θ = ω₀t + ½αt² — radians are mandatory
Thinking every point of a spinning wheel has the same linear speed — v = rω varies with radius
Believing an outward 'centrifugal force' really pushes you in an inertial frame — inertia carries you straight while the vehicle turns
Confusing rpm (revolutions per minute) with rad/s: multiply rpm by 2π/60 ≈ 0.105
Applying the constant-α equations to non-uniform spinning (a fan at steady speed has α = 0, not 'unknown')
applications: Gear and pulley design in Ethiopian workshops: rim speeds must match belt speeds
Washing-machine spin cycles and hard-drive platters rated in rpm
Banked road curves: the friction needed scales with v²/r
Earth's rotation: a point on the equator moves ≈ 465 m/s while the poles barely translate
g12-physics-up2-t2.summary: θ in radians, ω = Δθ/Δt, α = Δω/Δt, s = rθ and v = rω tie circles to straight lines; the kinematics equations transfer word for word. The outward push you feel is inertia, not a force.

questions.q: One complete revolution equals:
questions.explanation: The circumference is 2πr, and dividing by r gives 2π radians per full turn.

questions.q: The angular velocity of a body is defined as:
questions.explanation: ω = Δθ/Δt in rad/s; Δω/Δt would be α.

questions.q: The tangential speed of a point on a rotating wheel is:
questions.explanation: Arc per time: s/t = rθ/t = rω — outer points sweep faster.

questions.q: A wheel turns at 60 rpm. Its angular velocity is:
questions.explanation: 60 rpm = 1 rev/s, and 1 rev/s = 2π rad/s ≈ 6.28 rad/s.

questions.q: A fan speeds up uniformly from 4 rad/s to 10 rad/s in 3 s. Its α is:
questions.explanation: α = Δω/Δt = (10 − 4)/3 = 2 rad/s².

questions.q: The linear acceleration that mirrors v = v₀ + at for rotation is:
questions.explanation: Swap x↔θ, v↔ω, a↔α and the Unit-1 equation reappears unchanged.

questions.q: In a turning car you feel pushed toward the outside door because:
options: a centrifugal force acts outward in the ground frame
your inertia carries you straight while the car turns
questions.explanation: In the inertial frame no outward force exists; the car turns and the door intercepts your straight-line path.

questions.q: A wheel with ω₀ = 12 rad/s brakes at a constant α = −3 rad/s². Through how many revolutions does it turn before stopping?
questions.explanation: θ = ω₀²/(2|α|) = 144/6 = 24 rad to stop, and 24/(2π) ≈ 3.8 ≈ 4 revolutions.

g12-physics-up2-t3.overview: Torque is the turning effect of a force, and Newton's second law has a rotational twin: net torque changes angular momentum just as net force changes momentum. Flywheels, wrenches, seesaws and spinning skaters all obey this single extension of mechanics.
objectives: Define torque τ = rF sinθ and its sign convention
State rotational equilibrium: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0
Apply τ = Iα with moments of inertia
Use angular momentum L = Iω and its conservation
Solve seesaw, ladder and wheel problems
g12-physics-up2-t3.simple: Push at the right lever arm. The same 20 N on a 0.4 m wrench turns twice as hard as on a 0.2 m one — torque is force times perpendicular distance. A body at rest stays unrotating only if BOTH net force and net torque vanish. And a skater pulling arms in spins faster because angular momentum Iω refuses to change.
g12-physics-up2-t3.detailed:
Torque defined. τ = rF sinθ, where r runs from pivot to the point of force application and θ is the angle between them; equivalently τ = F × lever arm (perpendicular distance from pivot to the force line). Unit N·m — deliberately named joule-free to avoid confusion with energy: torque is a vector along the axis (right-hand rule), energy is a scalar.

Equilibrium (statics). Two conditions for no rotation and no translation: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0 about ANY point. Classic seesaw: m₁gx₁ = m₂gx₂ — a 30 kg child sits 2 m out, balancing a 60 kg child at 1 m. Ladder problems add friction at the floor; beam problems choose the pivot at an unknown reaction to delete it from the torque equation.

Newton's second law, rotated. τ_net = Iα, with moment of inertia I = Σmr² encoding how far mass sits from the axis: solid disc ½MR², hoop MR², sphere ⅖MR². Bigger I = harder to spin up, exactly like mass resists linear acceleration.

Angular momentum. L = Iω is conserved when net external torque is zero. The figure skater: arms out I large ω small; arms in I halves, ω doubles. L = mvr works for point masses too (a planet's orbital L), which foreshadows Kepler's second law.

Rotational energy. KE = ½Iω² — rolling bodies split it between translation and rotation, so a hoop (I = MR²) accelerates down slopes slower than a disc (½MR²): the race of the rolling shapes is an I-value contest, not a mass one.

keyTerms.def: L = Iω, conserved without external torque
equal opposite forces: pure torque, zero net force

workedExamples.problem: A 40 N force at 0.25 m from a hinge, perpendicular. Torque?
workedExamples.answer: 10 N·m opening the door.

workedExamples.problem: Seesaw: 25 kg at 1.6 m from fulcrum balances a 20 kg child at?
workedExamples.answer: 2 m — the lighter sits farther out.

workedExamples.problem: Skater: I = 3.6 kg·m² at ω = 2 rad/s pulls in to I = 1.2. New ω?
workedExamples.calculation: L = Iω = 3.6×2 = 7.2 kg·m²/s conserved; ω = 7.2/1.2 = 6 rad/s.
workedExamples.answer: 6 rad/s — three-fold spin-up, energy came from her muscles.

workedExamples.problem: A 2 kg solid disc (R = 0.1 m) spun up to 100 rad/s. Stored energy?
workedExamples.answer: 50 J — modest flywheel, the idea scales to tonnes.

commonMistakes: Taking r·F without the sinθ when the force is oblique
Balancing forces but forgetting to check torques (a body can translate AND rotate)
Calling N·m a joule for torque
Believing heavy objects roll faster (shape — I-value — decides, not mass)
Applying Iω conservation when external torque exists (brakes, friction)
applications: Cranes and balance: counter-torques keep booms level
Car engines: flywheels smooth the power strokes
Diving and figure skating: tucked rotations
Torque wrenches: calibrated N·m on wheel bolts
g12-physics-up2-t3.summary: Torque turns, I resists, L conserved: τ = rF sinθ, τ = Iα, I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ — the rotational Newton.

questions.q: Torque is maximum when the force is applied:
questions.explanation: sinθ = 1 at 90°.

questions.q: A body is in complete equilibrium when:
questions.explanation: Neither translation nor rotation may start.

questions.q: Moment of inertia depends on:
options: how mass is distributed about the axis
questions.explanation: Σmr²: distance from axis weighs the same mass more.

questions.q: Doubling the torque on a fixed wheel (constant I) doubles its:
questions.explanation: τ = Iα — acceleration scales, not instantaneous speed.

questions.q: A 50 N force on a 0.3 m spanner at 30° to the handle gives τ ≈:
Which reaches the bottom of a slope first from rest (same mass & radius)?
questions.explanation: Smallest I fraction (⅖MR²) — least energy locked in spin.

questions.q: A wheel spins freely; half its rim mass is removed (I halves). ω becomes:
questions.explanation: L = Iω conserved: halve I, double ω.

questions.q: Why choose the pivot ON an unknown force in statics?
options: its lever arm is zero, dropping it from the torque equation
questions.explanation: r = 0 makes τ = 0 regardless of magnitude — the standard elimination trick.

g12-physics-up2-t4.overview: Kepler read the planets' motions from Tycho's observations: ellipses, equal areas, and a precise period–distance ratio. Newton later proved all three are gravity's signature — and Kepler's third law still governs every orbit, from satellites to exoplanets.
objectives: State Kepler's three laws precisely
Describe ellipse geometry: semi-major axis, eccentricity
Apply the equal-areas law to speed variation
Use T² ∝ r³ for ratios and predictions
Connect Kepler to Newton's gravitation
g12-physics-up2-t4.simple: Three sentences that dethroned circles. Planets ride ellipses with the Sun at one focus. A line Sun-to-planet sweeps equal areas in equal times — so planets speed up near the Sun. And the square of the year is proportional to the cube of the mean distance. Data in 1609, proved by gravity 78 years later, still true for every moon and satellite.
g12-physics-up2-t4.detailed:
First law — ellipses. An ellipse has two foci; the Sun occupies one. Semi-major axis a is half the longest diameter; eccentricity e = c/a measures stretch (circle e = 0, Pluto-like e ≈ 0.25). Perihelion distance a(1−e), aphelion a(1+e). Copernicus kept circles-with-epicycles; Kepler trusted Tycho's 2 arcminute Mars residuals over beautiful geometry.

Second law — equal areas. The radius vector sweeps equal areas per unit time. At perihelion the short radius must sweep fast; at aphelion the long radius crawls. Physically this IS angular momentum conservation (L = ½m r²ω constant under a central force), with v_peri r_peri = v_ap r_ap.

Third law — harmonies. T² = (4π²/GM) a³: orbit period squared scales with mean distance cubed. In solar units (years, AU) it collapses to T² = a³ for planets around our Sun: Jupiter at 5.2 AU has T = 5.2^{1.5} ≈ 11.9 years. Around a different central mass, the ratio shifts — that is how we weigh stars and find exoplanets.

Newton's synthesis. Set gravitational force = centripetal need for circular orbits: GMm/r² = m(2π/T)²r → T² = 4π²r³/GM. Kepler's laws fall out of one inverse-square attraction; the ellipse appears when velocities exceed the circular value but stay bound. The same GM also yields orbital speed v = √(GM/r) and escape speed √2 times it.

keyTerms.def: force along the radius → L conserved

formulas.name: Third law
formulas.meaning: period and size are locked by central mass

formulas.name: Area law as L
formulas.meaning: fast when close, slow when far (perpendicular speeds)

formulas.name: Circular orbit speed
formulas.meaning: the one speed that curves with the field

workedExamples.problem: A planet orbits at 9 AU. Period in Earth years?
workedExamples.answer: 27 y — T² = a³ in solar units.

workedExamples.problem: Mars: perihelion 1.38 AU, aphelion 1.67 AU. e?
workedExamples.answer: e ≈ 0.095 — nearly circular.

workedExamples.problem: Geostationary orbit: T = 24 h. Radius?
workedExamples.answer: 42 200 km from centre = 35 800 km altitude.

workedExamples.problem: Comet 2× faster at perihelion than aphelion. Ratio r_p/r_a?
workedExamples.calculation: r_p v_p = r_a v_a → r_p/r_a = v_a/v_p = 1/2.
workedExamples.answer: Perihelion distance is half aphelion's.

commonMistakes: Saying the Sun sits at the centre of an ellipse (a focus)
Using T² ∝ r³ across different central masses without the GM factor
Confusing e (stretch) with orbit size
Forgetting geostationary altitude vs radius (−6 371 km)
Thinking equal-areas means constant speed
applications: Satellite placement: the geostationary radius is Kepler's third law, solved
Exoplanet detection: period + wobble = mass and orbit
Comet predictions (Halley returned 1758 on Newton–Kepler math)
Mars transfer windows: ellipses touch both orbits
g12-physics-up2-t4.summary: Ellipses at foci, equal areas per time, T² = a³: three observational facts Newton proved are one inverse-square law.

questions.q: Kepler's first law: orbits are:
questions.explanation: The ellipse replaced two millennia of perfect circles.

questions.q: A planet moves fastest at:
questions.explanation: Equal areas demand more speed for shorter radius.

questions.q: An asteroid at 4 AU has period:
Kepler's second law is the orbit form of conservation of:
questions.explanation: Central force ⇒ zero torque ⇒ L = ½mr²ω constant.

questions.q: Two moons of Jupiter have periods in ratio 1:8. Their orbital radii ratio is:
questions.explanation: r ∝ T^{2/3}: 8^{2/3} = 4 — the far moon orbits 4× out.

questions.q: If Earth's orbit e were 0, seasons of distance would:
questions.explanation: e = 0 is a circle: constant radius — and note real seasons come mainly from tilt.

questions.q: Third law's proportionality constant depends on:
questions.explanation: 4π²/GM — weigh the star by its planets.

questions.q: Newton derived Kepler from:
options: one inverse-square gravity + his motion laws
questions.explanation: Unification: falling apples and orbiting Moons, one force law.

g12-physics-up2-t5.overview: Gravitation is the universal attraction between masses — weakest of forces yet ruler of the cosmos. Newton's inverse-square law, the field concept, gravitational potential energy and escape velocity complete the mechanics that Kepler began.
objectives: Apply F = Gm₁m₂/r² to bodies and orbits
Define field strength g = GM/r² and vary with altitude
Distinguish g from G and weight from mass
Use potential energy U = −GMm/r (zero at infinity)
Derive and apply escape velocity v_e = √(2GM/R)
g12-physics-up2-t5.simple: The gentlest giant. G is a tiny number — 6.67×10⁻¹¹ — so gravity between everyday objects is negligible. But mass is everywhere and adds up, and inverse-square reach is infinite, so gravity alone steers galaxies. Double the distance, quarter the pull. Throw something faster than 11.2 km/s from Earth and it never returns: that is escape.
g12-physics-up2-t5.detailed:
The law. Every pair of point masses attracts along their line: F = Gm₁m₂/r². Spherically symmetric bodies (planets!) act as if all mass sat at their centre — Newton's shell theorem. Cavendish measured G (1798) with a torsion balance of lead balls, 'weighing the Earth': from g and R, M = gR²/G ≈ 6×10²⁴ kg.

Field strength. g = F/m = GM/r² — gravity as an invisible landscape assigning each point a force-per-kilogram. On Earth's surface 9.8 N/kg; at 6 400 km altitude it is 2.45 (quarter: twice Earth-radii out); at the Moon it is 1.6; inside a planet it falls toward zero (only the interior mass counts). Weight W = mg is the force; mass m is the inertia — never interchangeable.

Potential energy. U = −GMm/r with the conventional zero at infinite separation: bound orbits have negative total energy E = −GMm/2a. Lifting a mass increases U toward zero; falling releases the difference. This 'negative energy = captivity' language is exactly what escape bookkeeping uses.

Escape velocity. Set ½mv² = GMm/R: v_e = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR) — Earth: 11.2 km/s, Moon 2.4 km/s, Sun 618 km/s, a black hole's exceeds light so not even signals leave. Note: escape speed is a starting speed, not a sustained one — no rocket fuel needed after the launch if nothing hits it (real rockets go slower and thrust all the way).

Tides and limits. Gravity is differential: the Moon pulls the near ocean harder than the far side, stretching Earth into a slight egg — two bulges, twice-daily tides. Inverse-square plus finite size equals tidal forces, which also drive Io's volcanism and can shred comets (Roche limit).

keyTerms.def: difference of gravity across a body

formulas.name: Orbit ↔ Kepler
formulas.meaning: orbit speed and gravity lock together

vars.meaning: mass of orbited body from moons

workedExamples.problem: Weight of 70 kg at twice Earth-radius altitude?
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 172 N (a 17 kg-feeling of 70 kg mass).

workedExamples.problem: Find Earth's mass from g = 9.8, R = 6.4×10⁶ m.
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 6.0×10²⁴ kg — Cavendish's harvest.

workedExamples.problem: Escape speed from the Moon (M = 7.35×10²² kg, R = 1.74×10⁶ m)?
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 2.4 km/s — why the Moon kept no air.

workedExamples.problem: A satellite's orbit radius quadruples. Its period factor?
workedExamples.answer: 8× longer (Kepler again, from gravitation).

commonMistakes: Quoting g at altitude using r from the SURFACE instead of the centre
Mixing G (constant) with g (local field)
Saying astronauts float because 'there is no gravity' in orbit — they are falling with the ship
Treating escape speed as a continuous thrust requirement
Forgetting U is negative for bound systems (zero means free-and-stopped)
applications: Geostationary and GPS orbits: GM is the design number
Locating ore bodies with tiny g-anomalies (gravimetry)
The Ethiopian highlands' slightly lower g (altitude) matters in precision weighing
Tidal energy and the Moon slowly receding (3.8 cm/yr)
g12-physics-up2-t5.summary: F = Gm₁m₂/r² rules everything at range: g = GM/r², U = −GMm/r, escape at √(2gR). Weak, but infinite and additive.

questions.q: Doubling the separation of two masses makes the force:
questions.explanation: Inverse square: 2² = 4 down.

questions.q: The value of G is:
questions.explanation: The gravitational constant; 9.8 is Earth's g.

questions.q: In a falling orbiting spacecraft, astronauts float because:
options: they and the ship accelerate identically
questions.explanation: Free fall: gravity supplies exactly the centripetal motion — 'weightless' ≠ 'gravityless'.

questions.q: Earth's g at 3R from centre is:
Which weighs more on the Moon vs Earth?
questions.explanation: Mass constant; weight = mg shrinks to ⅙.

questions.q: Escape speed scales with planet radius and g as:
questions.explanation: ½mv² = mgR (surface form) ⇒ v = √(2gR).

questions.q: U = −GMm/r being negative signals:
options: a bound state: energy must be added to free it
questions.explanation: Zero at infinity is freedom; negative = in the well.

questions.q: Two ocean bulges (facing and opposite the Moon) exist because:
questions.explanation: Near side pulled harder than centre, far side pulled less — the egg deformation.
